notable_claims: The University of Nebraska-Lincoln banned all alt.* newsgroups.
Switzerland's SWITCH consortium blocked NNTP, telnet, and FTP packets to local eunet chapters.
University of Cincinnati terminated accounts for users accessing 'game' and IRC hosts.
UIC computing resource penalties were critiqued as vague and severe, allowing arbitrary enforcement.
classification.summary: This is a digest abstract summarizing various reports on academic computing policies and censorship from March 1992. It highlights conflicts over the banning of alt.* newsgroups at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, network blocking by SWITCH in Switzerland, and critiques of restrictive computer use policies at the University of Delaware and UIC.
classification.title: Article 0 -- Abstract of CAF-News 02.22

notable_claims: The decision to remove alt groups was made after a meeting of the UNL Academic Senate Computational Services and Facilities Committee.
Administration claimed memory usage on UNLINFO was doubling every four months.
Concerns were raised regarding potential violations of state pornography laws.
organizations: UNL Academic Senate Computational Services and Facilities Committee
classification.summary: A student newspaper article reports on the University of Nebraska-Lincoln's decision to stop feeding 'alt.*' Usenet newsgroups into the UNLINFO system. Administration cited resource constraints and the presence of pornographic content as reasons for the removal. Students argued that many alternative groups were legitimate forums for discussion.
classification.title: Newspaper article at U. of Nebraska (alts)

identity.subject: Article 1--Newspaper article at U. of Nebraska (alts)

notable_claims: The removal of the alt.* hierarchy is viewed as an extreme measure that could discourage excellent students from enrolling.
Usenet has emerged as an essential core facility for universities to support their educational and research missions.
classification.summary: Kent Landfield wrote an open letter protesting the University of Nebraska-Lincoln (UNL) Computing Resource Center's decision to remove the 'alt.*' Usenet newsgroup hierarchy. He argues that restricting access to these groups harms the university's academic competitiveness and mission. Landfield suggests that if resource constraints are the issue, the university should seek more funding rather than censoring content.
classification.title: An Open Letter to UNL CRC: Removal of alt.*

identity.subject: Article 2--An Open Letter to UNL CRC: Removal of alt.*

notable_claims: Usenet is not a legal right or public utility, but depends on the owners of the hardware carrying the traffic.
SWITCH removed various Usenet newsgroups without prior notice via administrative fiat.
SWITCH previously blocked port 25 (SMTP) to force the use of X.400 software.
SWITCH was blocking NNTP, Telnet, and FTP packets to local EUnet chapters.
organizations: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne
classification.summary: Mitchell Wyle discusses the restriction of Usenet newsgroups and network protocols by SWITCH, the Swiss networking entity. The post includes a lengthy quote from Chip Salzenberg arguing that Usenet is not a right or public utility, but subject to the property rights of machine owners. Wyle provides technical evidence of SWITCH blocking specific ports (NNTP, Telnet, FTP) to local EUnet sites.
classification.title: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

identity.subject: Article 3--Re: Censorship and bigotry come up strong in Switzerland

notable_claims: Student inaction regarding service shutdowns is often due to a belief that petitions will not effect change.
Administrators should facilitate user involvement in policy-making rather than acting arbitrarily.
classification.summary: Sean Casey responds to Mark Hittinger regarding the shutdown of controversial network services. Casey argues that a lack of student petitions does not imply a lack of seriousness, but rather a systemic distrust of authority. He advocates for administrators to be less arbitrary and more inclusive in policy-making processes.
classification.title: Article 4--Re: Why I hate IRC

notable_claims: The UDel policy allows system administrators to suspend computing privileges during an investigation, which may conflict with student rights regarding status changes pending charges.
The policy defines the individual or department as the 'Data Owner' rather than the University.
System administrators are authorized to inspect user files without permission in cases of imminent danger to the system or suspected malicious intent.
The policy prohibits use of resources for purposes other than those intended, creating ambiguity regarding non-disruptive personal use.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides a detailed critique of the University of Delaware's proposed 'Responsible Computing Policy.' He analyzes the policy's approach to user participation, due process regarding account suspension, privacy rights over data, and restrictions on personal use. Kadie argues for clearer distinctions between protecting university property and punishing users before conviction.
classification.title: Status of UDel's Responsible Computing Policy

identity.subject: Article 5--Re: [eff.mail.ethics-l] Status of UDel's Responsible Computing Policy

notable_claims: The UIC policy's ban on unsolicited communications is so broad it could penalize system operators for quota warnings.
Accessing another person's account units or disk storage (e.g., viewing a .login file with permission) carries a minimum 3-month suspension.
The policy grants the Computer Center expansive discretion, creating an illusion of due process while remaining arbitrary.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the University of Illinois at Chicago's (UIC) computing resources penalties policy, arguing it is overbroad and repressive. He highlights specific rules regarding unsolicited messages and account usage that he claims lead to arbitrary enforcement and disproportionate punishment. The critique contrasts the policy with a Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students.
classification.title: Re: U of Illinois at Chicago Penalties Policy

identity.subject: Article 6--Re: U of Illinois at Chicago Penalties Policy

notable_claims: Some admins believe email searches are more invasive than physical searches because they leave no trace.
There is disagreement on whether written policies protect employees or make them targets for termination by supervisors.
Opinions differ on whether universities should establish privacy policies before legal precedents are settled via court cases.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie shares paraphrased responses from system administrators regarding the ethics and authorization of searching user emails and files at universities. The discussion contrasts technical maintenance with surveillance and debates whether written policies protect admins or expose them to legal risk. It highlights a tension between administrative authority and individual privacy in early academic computing environments.
classification.title: How do U. of I. sys admins feel about email privacy for users?

identity.subject: Article 7--Re: How do U. of I. sys admins feel about email privacy for users?

notable_claims: Email privacy is not guaranteed in the provided corporate/government policy
Privacy may be breached during termination, security breaches, or extended absences
classification.summary: A user shares an example of an RS/6000 access request sheet from their employer to illustrate email privacy policies. The document outlines specific conditions under which email privacy may be breached, such as termination of employment or security research. It explicitly states that while the organization attempts to preserve privacy, it cannot be guaranteed.
classification.title: Article 8--Re: EMAIL PRIVACY

notable_claims: Anonymous FTP at uu.net is a myth as users must be identifiable.
All file transfers on ftp.uu.net are logged.
Incoming files are screened for security problems and copyright infringement.
Access is denied to hosts involved in security or copyright violations.
classification.summary: James Revell Jr. describes the restrictive access and monitoring policies implemented at ftp.uu.net to combat abuse. The system requires identifiable users via PTR records and email addresses, while logging all file transfers. Revell justifies these measures as necessary for security and to avoid legal liability regarding copyright infringement.
classification.title: Logging usage of services (FTP)

notable_claims: Making offensive information available in a library does not typically create an illegal hostile environment.
Students and professors generally have broad freedom to make offensive comments if they are related to the subject matter in a classroom context.
Private sexual harassment or pursuing someone who wants to be left alone can be grounds for punishment.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie and Professor Louise Fitzgerald discuss the legal distinctions between providing access to offensive materials in a library versus creating a hostile environment through targeted harassment. They contrast the protections afforded to academic materials and classroom discourse with the punishable nature of private sexual harassment.
classification.title: Network distribution of Pornographic material

identity.subject: Article 10--Re: Network distribution of Pornographic material.
